result: This phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 120 HIV-uninfected adults with TBM at a hospital in Vietnam between October 2014 and May 2016. Participants were randomized 1:1:1 to receive placebo (n=41), aspirin 81 mg/day (n=39), or aspirin 1000 mg/day (n=40) for 60 days, in addition to standard anti-tuberculosis drugs and dexamethasone. The trial used appropriate randomization, blinding, and stratification methods, with pre-specified analysis plans.
evaluation: The trial design and conduct are well-documented with appropriate methodology (C86-C88, C113-C117). Enrollment, randomization, and follow-up data are clearly reported (C4, C36-C40). The trial was properly registered (C120), ethically approved (C82), and monitored by an independent safety board (C118). Sample size justification is provided with power calculations (C103-C110).

result: At baseline, 92/120 (76.7%) participants had microbiologically confirmed TBM, and 40/114 (35.1%) had at least one brain infarct on MRI. The placebo and aspirin 1000 mg groups had higher proportions with baseline infarcts (42.5% and 38.5% respectively) than the aspirin 81 mg group (22.9%).
evaluation: These baseline characteristics are directly reported from the trial data (C5, C6, C45). The imbalance in baseline infarcts across groups is acknowledged and could potentially confound efficacy analyses, though randomization should have minimized systematic bias.

result: The primary safety outcome (gastro-intestinal or cerebral bleeding by day 60) occurred in 5/36 (13.9%) placebo, 8/35 (22.9%) aspirin 81 mg, and 8/40 (20.0%) aspirin 1000 mg participants (p=0.59). Only one new cerebral bleed occurred. Most bleeding events (16/20; 80%) were grade 1-2, and none required active management. Overall, aspirin was not associated with a significant increase in grade 3-4 or serious adverse events.
evaluation: The safety data are clearly reported with appropriate statistical comparisons (C7, C68-C71). The finding of no significant increase in serious bleeding is supported by the data, though the non-significant trend toward more minor bleeding events (C51, C128) warrants consideration. The trial was underpowered to definitively rule out rare but serious bleeding complications.

result: In the intention-to-treat population, the primary efficacy outcome (new MRI-proven brain infarction or death by day 60) occurred in 11/38 (28.9%) placebo, 8/36 (22.2%) aspirin 81 mg, and 6/38 (15.8%) aspirin 1000 mg participants (p=0.40). The observed risk of new brain infarction was lower in aspirin-treated patients (p=0.18), and 60% of baseline infarcts in the aspirin 1000 mg group resolved by day 60 versus 14.2% in aspirin 81 mg and 42.9% in placebo (p=0.14).
evaluation: While the data show trends favoring aspirin, particularly the 1000 mg dose, none of the primary efficacy comparisons reached statistical significance (C8, C53, C54). The trial was explicitly not powered to show definitive efficacy (C74, C105). Missing data for 15 subjects on the primary endpoint (C39) and baseline imbalances in infarct prevalence (C45) further complicate interpretation.

result: In the per-protocol population (n=98), new infarction or death by day 60 occurred in 10/34 (29.4%) placebo, 6/31 (19.3%) aspirin 81 mg, and 3/30 (10.0%) aspirin 1000 mg participants (p=0.16). No deaths occurred in the aspirin 1000 mg group versus 13% and 11% in aspirin 81 mg and placebo groups (p=0.11).
evaluation: The per-protocol analysis shows stronger trends favoring aspirin 1000 mg (C56-C58), but still does not reach statistical significance. The exclusion of 22 participants (C40) who received <30 days of study drug introduces potential bias, as those who stopped treatment may have differed systematically from those who continued. The suggestion of benefit (C131) requires cautious interpretation.

result: Planned subgroup analysis showed a significant interaction between aspirin treatment effect and diagnostic category (P_heterogeneity=0.01). In participants with microbiologically confirmed TBM, aspirin suggested a potential reduction in new infarcts and deaths by day 60: 11/32 (34.4%) placebo vs. 4/27 (14.8%) aspirin 81 mg vs. 3/28 (10.7%) aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.06). The effect was most marked for aspirin 1000 mg (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.06-0.93, p=0.039), with a number-needed-to-treat of 4.
evaluation: The subgroup analysis was pre-specified (C9, C59), which strengthens its validity. The significant interaction term (P=0.01) and the p=0.039 for aspirin 1000 mg vs placebo in confirmed TBM (C60) are notable. However, this is a subgroup analysis with multiple comparisons, increasing the risk of false positives. The p=0.06 for the overall comparison in this subgroup (C10) is borderline. The finding requires confirmation in a larger trial powered for this specific population.

result: In the ITT population, there was no significant difference in death or disability by day 60 or 8 months across treatment groups. Eight-month mortality was 11.9% overall: 12.8% placebo, 15.4% aspirin 81 mg, and 7.5% aspirin 1000 mg (p=0.50). In the per-protocol population, there was a trend to better 8-month outcomes in the aspirin 1000 mg group (p=0.13). Hydrocephalus by day 60 was less common in the aspirin 1000 mg group (5.3%) than aspirin 81 mg (15.6%) and placebo (22.9%) (p=0.09).
evaluation: The secondary outcomes show consistent trends favoring aspirin 1000 mg but lack statistical significance (C62-C66). The trial was not powered for these endpoints (C74). The trend toward reduced hydrocephalus (C66) is interesting but requires confirmation. The lack of effect on disability despite potential mortality benefit suggests complex disease mechanisms.

result: CSF analysis demonstrated aspirin dose-dependent inhibition of thromboxane A2 (measured as TXB2) and upregulation of pro-resolving protectins. Partial least squares discriminant analysis of day 30 CSF showed clustering of lipid mediators by treatment group. Comparing baseline to day 30, significant differences in TXB2 inhibition and protectin upregulation were observed in the aspirin 1000 mg group versus placebo.
evaluation: The CSF lipid mediator analysis provides mechanistic support for aspirin's effects (C11, C12, C72, C73). The dose-dependent effects on TXB2 and protectins are clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical methods (Figure 3). This mechanistic data strengthens the biological plausibility of the clinical findings, though it does not directly prove clinical benefit.

result: The authors conclude that daily aspirin 81 mg or 1000 mg can be given safely with dexamethasone and anti-tuberculosis drugs for HIV-uninfected adults with TBM. The trial provides evidence that aspirin induces dose-dependent inhibition of TXA2 and upregulation of protectins in the CNS, which may reduce brain infarcts and improve outcomes. These findings support conducting a large phase 3 trial of adjunctive aspirin for TBM.
evaluation: The conclusion regarding safety is well-supported by the data (C7, C68-C71, C127). The mechanistic findings are robust (C11-C12, C72-C73, C140). However, the authors appropriately acknowledge the trial was not powered for definitive efficacy (C74, C105) and that clinical findings require cautious interpretation (C139). The recommendation for a phase 3 trial is justified given the safety profile, mechanistic data, and suggestive efficacy signals.

result: The trial had important limitations: assessment of the primary efficacy endpoint required participants to be well enough for MRI at baseline and day 60. Three screened patients were too unwell for baseline imaging, and five participants were too unwell for day 60 imaging. Therefore, findings may not be generalizable to those with very severe disease at baseline.
evaluation: This is an important and appropriately acknowledged limitation (C123-C126). The exclusion of the most severely ill patients (who may have the most to gain or lose from treatment) limits generalizability. This selection bias is inherent to the imaging-based primary endpoint and should be considered when interpreting results.

result: Combining dexamethasone with aspirin did not significantly increase severe gastro-intestinal bleeding, though there was a non-significant increase in minor (grade 1-2) bleeding events. The risk of severe gastric bleeding appears very low. The per-protocol analysis suggested participants who received >30 days of aspirin may benefit more than those who stopped earlier, suggesting future management of minor bleeding could be less conservative.
evaluation: The safety conclusion is supported (C127), but the interpretation regarding duration of treatment (C131) is speculative. The per-protocol analysis is subject to bias since participants who stopped treatment may have differed from those who continued. The recommendation for less conservative management of minor bleeding (C130) requires validation in a larger trial before implementation.

result: The findings are compared to two previous trials: an Indian trial (Misra et al., 2010) showing aspirin with prednisolone reduced brain infarcts and mortality, and a South African pediatric trial (Schoeman et al., 2011) showing no benefit. The authors conclude that data from all three trials suggest aspirin at doses from 81-1000 mg/day can be safely added to anti-tuberculosis and corticosteroid therapy, with higher doses likely more effective.
evaluation: The comparison to prior trials is appropriate (C132-C135), but the synthesis requires caution. The Indian trial had methodological issues with variable corticosteroid use (C32-C33), and the pediatric trial showed no benefit (C35). The conclusion that higher doses are more effective (C137) is based on trends in the current trial and indirect comparisons across different populations. A definitive dose-finding study is needed.

result: The authors establish the clinical context: TBM kills or disables around half of sufferers, dexamethasone reduces mortality but not disability, and cerebral infarction is the commonest cause of irreversible neurological injury. TBM-related infarcts are caused by a combination of vasospasm, intimal proliferation, and thrombosis, though the role of thrombosis remains controversial.
evaluation: These background claims are well-supported by appropriate citations (C1, C2, C14-C21). The characterization of TBM pathophysiology and the rationale for investigating anti-thrombotic therapy are sound. The acknowledgment of controversy regarding thrombosis (C19-C20) is appropriate.

result: The authors hypothesize that aspirin prevents TBM-related brain infarction through anti-thrombotic, anti-inflammatory, and pro-resolution properties. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase, with anti-inflammatory effects at >600 mg/day and anti-thrombotic effects at lower doses. Aspirin uniquely triggers production of pro-resolving mediators (15-epi-lipoxins, 17R-resolvins, protectins) not shared by other NSAIDs or corticosteroids.
evaluation: The hypothesis is well-grounded in established pharmacology (C22-C29) with appropriate citations. The rationale for testing two doses (81 mg for anti-thrombotic effects, 1000 mg for anti-inflammatory effects) is sound. The unique pro-resolution properties of aspirin (C29) provide additional mechanistic rationale beyond simple anti-platelet effects.

result: The authors interpret that aspirin's benefit may be driven by upregulation of pro-resolving molecules, supported by the finding that 60% of baseline infarcts in the aspirin 1000 mg group resolved by day 60 versus 14.2% in aspirin 81 mg and 42.9% in placebo. The CSF analysis showing dose-dependent TXA2 inhibition and protectin upregulation supports this mechanism.
evaluation: The mechanistic interpretation linking protectin upregulation to infarct resolution (C76, C140) is plausible but speculative. While the CSF data clearly show biochemical effects (C73), and the imaging shows differential infarct resolution (C54), the causal connection is not definitively established. The p=0.14 for infarct resolution (C54) indicates this could be due to chance. Alternative explanations for infarct resolution are not fully explored.

result: The authors suggest the findings may have relevance for treatment of other forms of tuberculosis, adding to evidence that aspirin and other NSAIDs may be useful adjunctive agents in tuberculosis treatment generally.
evaluation: This extrapolation beyond TBM (C80, C141) is highly speculative. While the citation to Kroesen et al., 2017 provides some support, the mechanisms of disease and potential benefits of aspirin likely differ substantially between TBM and pulmonary or other forms of tuberculosis. This claim requires independent investigation and should not be inferred from the current TBM-specific data.
